stories.title: Self-hosted distributed durable objects run without central consensus
stories.social_post:
Running distributed stateful workloads usually forces a trade-off between complex consensus clusters and centralized coordination bottlenecks.

Celld takes an unconventional architectural route to run Cloudflare Workers and Durable Objects on self-hosted infrastructure. Instead of deploying Raft or etcd to manage node membership and leader election, every celld daemon coordinates state purely through conditional writes against an object storage bucket such as S3. A conditional write establishes exclusive ownership of a cell, turning the cloud storage provider into the arbiter of lease management.

Under this model, each cell operates as an isolated server backed by its own local SQLite database. Writes are captured and serialized into the LTX replication format, while peer-to-peer communication runs over signed HTTP requests. When a node crashes or relinquishes a cell, another node can assume ownership by acquiring the lock in object storage and pulling the latest transaction logs.

Decoupling execution from centralized control planes proves that distributed primitives do not always require heavy distributed consensus.
stories.why_read: Read this to understand how celld coordinates distributed state using conditional bucket writes instead of dedicated consensus clusters. You will learn how it combines V8 and SQLite to run self-hosted Cloudflare Workers primitives.

stories.title: Switching Envoy to oghttp2 caused severe HTTP/2 performance regressions
stories.social_post:
Upgrading Envoy to version 1.34 triggered an unexpected twenty percent drop in HTTP/2 throughput across customer proxies. The culprit was not a configuration blunder or connection leak, but a quiet change in the underlying default codec from nghttp2 to Google oghttp2.

Flamegraphs across multiple CPU microarchitectures revealed where the cycles vanished. While nghttp2 relies on lean C data structures with caller-provided buffers, oghttp2 imports complex abstractions from the QUICHE family originally built for HTTP/3. In high-volume proxy workloads, the extra allocation overhead and less optimized Huffman header decoding accumulated into a massive performance penalty.

Envoy maintainers eventually rolled back the default codec in version 1.37 after numerous teams flagged fifteen to twenty-five percent latency regressions.

Modern shared libraries often promise unified codebases across protocols, but protocol convergence should never come at the expense of baseline CPU efficiency.
stories.why_read: Read this to understand the low-level architectural reasons why Envoy's switch from nghttp2 to oghttp2 caused significant CPU and throughput regressions. It offers a detailed, flamegraph-driven breakdown of HTTP/2 codec overhead and header processing.

stories.title: Self-hosted durable objects drastically reduce high scale infrastructure costs
stories.social_post:
Cloudflare Durable Objects solved stateful serverless computing, but tying your distributed architecture to a proprietary edge runtime introduces severe lock-in and steep operational bills.

Celld changes this equation by introducing an open-source, self-hosted runtime that executes Cloudflare Workers and Durable Objects across arbitrary virtual machines while persisting data directly into standard object storage.

The architectural profile is remarkably lean. Each resident cell requires just 0.47 megabytes of memory, allowing an eight-gigabyte host node to sustain around 2,500 active cells. Warm stateless execution achieves sub-millisecond p99 latencies, while hibernated cells wake up in approximately 4 milliseconds.

Distributed correctness relies on epoch-fenced single writers per cell. This design ensures that failover takes roughly 20 seconds with zero acknowledged write loss, delivering a recovery point objective of zero across node terminations.

Decoupling stateful coordination from specialized edge vendors gives backend engineers full control over data sovereignty without sacrificing the convenience of the actor model.
stories.why_read: Read this to understand how celld runs self-hosted durable objects with zero data loss at significantly lower operational costs. You will discover its performance benchmarks, including memory density, write latencies, and failover mechanics.

stories.title: Exponent alignment enables ultra-fast lossless compression for BF16 KV cache
stories.social_post:
Transferring key-value caches across PCIe links or network interfaces is frequently the dominant bottleneck for time-to-first-token in large language model inference. When serving long contexts, memory bandwidth and transfer speeds constrain throughput far more than raw matrix arithmetic.

ExANS tackles this limitation by introducing a lossless graphics processing unit codec tailored for 16-bit brain floating-point tensors. Rather than running standard compression across high-entropy floating-point data, the algorithm isolates the 8-bit exponent field from the combined sign and mantissa. Because cached attention tensors share structural similarity across heads and layers, their exponent ranges exhibit narrow local clustering.

By centering these exponents and applying GPU-accelerated asymmetric numeral systems, ExANS achieves a 1.51x lossless compression ratio while decoding at 622 gigabytes per second on an Nvidia H100. Because decode throughput outpaces the physical bandwidth of standard interconnects, cached tensor blocks arrive in compute memory faster than raw uncompressed transmission.

Optimizing system throughput does not always require lossy quantization when domain-specific data layouts expose predictable structural patterns.
stories.why_read: Learn how ExANS exploits low-entropy exponent fields in BF16 tensors to achieve ultra-fast lossless decompression on GPUs. This post explains how targeted entropy coding overcomes PCIe and network bandwidth bottlenecks to reduce time-to-first-token in inference engines.

stories.title: Scaling rollout inference independently accelerates agentic reinforcement learning
stories.social_post:
Agentic reinforcement learning runs into a fundamental infrastructure mismatch when scaling trainer compute alone. During training runs for multi-turn coding agents, rollout generation consumes the vast majority of wall-clock step time. While worker nodes wait for an inference engine to complete multi-step environment executions, expensive training accelerators sit completely idle.

The solution is disaggregating the inference fleet from the training cluster. In a recent benchmark training a Qwen model on bug-fixing tasks with the slime framework, researchers decoupled three SGLang inference engines from the trainer using SkyPilot Job Groups. Scaling rollout capacity independently dropped the asynchronous step time from 1200 seconds down to 661 seconds, nearly doubling throughput without touching the trainer configuration.

Modern post-training has evolved from single-shot preference pairs into interactive, multi-turn agent execution inside sandbox environments like microVMs. Treating rollout generation as an elastic distributed inference problem rather than a side effect of training unlocks massive efficiency gains.

If your reinforcement learning cluster is stalling, stop adding training compute and scale your rollout inference instead.
stories.why_read: Read this to understand why rollout generation bottlenecks agentic reinforcement learning and how decoupling inference from training cuts step time in half.

stories.title: Measuring real-world behavior in modern copy-on-write filesystems
stories.social_post:
Standard filesystem benchmarks often mislead because they run simple synthetic fio workloads on a single, clean disk. That approach reveals almost nothing about how modern copy-on-write filesystems such as ZFS, btrfs, or bcachefs behave under sustained production pressure.

The Modern-Fs-Benchmark suite addresses this limitation by testing multi-device filesystems across actual operational edge cases. Instead of measuring only raw sequential throughput, it evaluates trivial-operation latency during write saturation, such as a four-kilobyte write and fsync every 200 milliseconds while a streaming process floods disk I/O. This test isolates copy-on-write commit storms and exposes severe p99 tail latencies that traditional benchmarks miss completely.

The test harness also tracks snapshot degradation over time, degraded array rebuilds, self-healing under bit rot, and behavior near disk exhaustion.

If you manage storage engines or host stateful databases, these benchmarks provide the exact failure modes and latency cliffs you must account for in production.
stories.why_read: Read this to understand how modern multi-device filesystems perform under realistic stress conditions like snapshot aging and fsync tail latency. You will gain insight into the actual operational trade-offs that conventional benchmarks fail to capture.
